passages.happening:
Abijah becomes king of Judah and reigns three years; ‘there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam’ (verse 2). Abijah's army of 400,000 faces Jeroboam's 800,000 (verse 3). Standing on Mount Zemaraim, Abijah calls out, “Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel!” (verse 4). ‘Do you not know that the LORD, the God of Israel, has given the kingship of Israel to David and his descendants forever by a covenant of salt?’ (verse 5).

He charges that Jeroboam rebelled, and that the north now has golden calves for gods and has driven out the priests of the LORD: ‘Now whoever comes to consecrate himself with a young bull and seven rams can become a priest of things that are not gods’ (verse 9). “But as for us, the LORD is our God. We have not forsaken Him” (verse 10). Judah keeps the morning and evening offerings, the showbread and the lamps (verse 11). He ends, “O children of Israel, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you will not succeed” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Rehoboam's son Abijah reigns about 913 to 911 BC, and the Chronicler gives his reign a single scene: a battle framed by a speech that states the Chronicler's own convictions. The north has the numbers; the south has the covenant with David and the temple's worship.

The speech works like a sermon with a legal case: a claim, that the kingdom belongs to David's line; a charge, that Jeroboam rebelled and set up false priests and gods; a defense, that Judah has kept the LORD's worship; and an appeal, do not fight against the LORD. A covenant of salt meant a lasting, unbreakable agreement; salt preserves and does not decay, and it was added to Israel's grain offerings as the salt of the covenant. The mockery of a priesthood open to anyone with a bull and seven rams sets Jeroboam's priests against the law's limit of priesthood to Aaron's line.

Kings calls him Abijam and gives a brief, negative verdict. The Chronicler does not contradict it so much as leave it unmentioned and show one moment when Abijah spoke and acted rightly. Some think he drew on another source, since he cites the prophet Iddo in verse 22; others see Abijah here chiefly as a voice for the claims of David's house and the Jerusalem temple.
passages.later: Kings says of him, ‘And Abijam walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed’ (1 Kings 15:3).
passages.hard:
Are the numbers in this battle, 400,000, 800,000 and 500,000 slain, meant literally?

The figures are very large for the region at the time, and readers handle them in several ways. Some take them as accurate counts. Others note that the Hebrew word eleph, usually translated thousand, can also mean a clan or a military unit, so the numbers may first have counted units, giving much smaller totals. Others see them as round, heightened figures expressing the scale of the conflict and of God's deliverance, in keeping with ancient battle reports. Copying errors in numbers are also possible. A related puzzle is Abijah's mother, Micaiah daughter of Uriel here and Maacah daughter of Abishalom in 1 Kings 15:2; explanations include two names for one woman, or Maacah being a granddaughter of Absalom through Uriel. The site's page on the numbers in Samuel, Kings and Chronicles sets out these ways. On any view the chapter's point stands: a smaller force that relied on God prevailed over a larger one.
passages.asks: Abijah called the northerners children of Israel and begged them not to fight against God. Ask whether you can disagree with someone and still call them family. And ask which of your own claims to be on God's side would survive the test of your actual worship.

passages.happening:
Jeroboam sends an ambush around behind Judah (verse 13). ‘When Judah turned and discovered that the battle was both before and behind them, they cried out to the LORD. Then the priests blew the trumpets’ (verse 14), and the men raise the battle cry, and God routs Jeroboam and all Israel (verse 15). ‘Thus the Israelites were subdued at that time, and the men of Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers’ (verse 18).

Abijah takes Bethel and other towns (verse 19). Jeroboam never recovers his power in Abijah's days, ‘and the LORD struck him down and he died’ (verse 20). Abijah grows strong (verse 21), and his acts are written in the writings of the prophet Iddo (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The story pays off every claim of the speech: the ambush puts Judah in danger, they cry out, tsa'aq, the word for the cry of the oppressed; the priests blow the silver trumpets, chatsotserah, as the law commanded in battle; God routs Israel; and verse 18 gives the lesson, that Judah relied, sha'an, on the LORD. The verb means to put one's weight on a support, and it will come back in Asa's story.

Mount Zemaraim lay in the hill country of Ephraim near the border. Bethel was one of Jeroboam's two royal shrines with a golden calf, so taking it was a symbolic blow as well as a military one, though it later returned to northern control.

The battle is between brothers. Abijah's speech calls the northerners children of Israel, and the Chronicler, writing for a community that still hoped for all Israel, never forgets it.
passages.later: The law had said of the trumpets, ‘you will be remembered before the LORD your God and saved from your enemies’ (Numbers 10:9). A psalm says, ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God’ (Psalm 20:7).
passages.asks: Surrounded, Judah cried out and relied on God. Ask where you are surrounded right now. And ask what it would look like to put your full weight on God there, rather than on your own strength.
